problem: The sentence "Cells past the last non-blank are all □, so we never write them" is stated for the whole ID, but a blank cell can lie between the last non-blank and the head. If those blanks are left out of α, the head position is lost and two different snapshots get the same ID. Example: tape 1, head on cell 2 in state q0 must be 1□q0; written as 1q0 it wrongly says the head is on cell 1.
fix: Scope the rule to the right end only: "Blanks to the right of the head are never written. Blanks to the left of the head stay in α, because they record how far right the head has gone: tape 1 with the head on cell 2 is 1□q0, not 1q0."

problem: Step 3 gives the ID as 10q2□ and then says it is "written 10q2 when the trailing blanks are dropped". The □ there is the scanned cell, not a trailing blank, and the exam trap in the same chapter says the scanned □ must not be dropped. Step 3, the answer line (which uses 10q2□) and the trap contradict each other, so a student cannot tell which form to write in the exam.
fix: Choose one convention and keep it everywhere. Either always keep the scanned cell (the run reads q000 ⊢ 1q10 ⊢ 10q2□ ⊢ 1qaccept0, and Q5 ends at 01qaccept□), or state once that β may be empty and that 10q2 means the head sits on a blank cell, then delete the "do not drop the scanned cell" half of the trap.

problem: "Several labels may share one arrow when they differ only in the symbol read" is too narrow. Two labels may also differ in the symbol written and still use one arrow, provided the destination state and the direction are the same.
fix: "Several labels may share one arrow when they have the same destination and the same direction, even if they differ in the symbol read and the symbol written, for example '0 → 1, R' and '1 → 0, R' on the same arrow."

problem: "the number of distinct IDs a small machine visits is the object of study" misdescribes busy-beaver search. That search maximises the number of steps (and of 1s left on the tape) before halting; the count of distinct IDs is only the bound used to conclude that a machine has entered a loop.
fix: "the number of steps a small machine runs before it halts is the object of study, and a machine that visits more distinct IDs than it has configurations can never halt."

problem: The chapter says a left move from the leftmost cell is "not allowed" but never says what the model does when a transition asks for one, so the definition of a move is incomplete at the left end of the tape.
fix: "The tape is unbounded only to the right. If δ(q, a) = (p, b, L) and the head is on the leftmost cell, the move is illegal; treat δ on that pair as undefined, so the machine halts there. A correct design never asks for such a move."
